topics: 💰 Selling Meat That Turns Out Forbidden — firstborn, tereifa, untithed produce, and idolatrous wine compared
🤢 Repulsive vs. Non-Repulsive — why the buyer of firstborn meat gets only a partial refund
📜 New Chapter: Deriving the Blemishes from 'Lame or Blind... Any Ill Blemish'
👂 Blemishes of the Ear — torn cartilage, splits, holes the size of a karshina, and a desiccated ear
📏 How Big Is a Karshina? — comparing measurements to the laws of ritual impurity

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing One Chapter, Opening the List of Blemishes
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 37a–37b
overview.hebrewSource: עַל אֵלּוּ מוּמִין שׁוֹחֲטִין אֶת הַבְּכוֹר: נִפְגְּמָה אׇזְנוֹ מִן הַחַסְחוּס, אֲבָל לֹא הָעוֹר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes the chapter on disqualified consecrated animals with a mishna on selling meat that turns out to have been forbidden all along — a slaughtered firstborn never shown to a Sage, or a cow that turns out to be a tereifa — and works out exactly how much of a refund the buyer is owed. A new chapter then opens with the Torah's own list of disqualifying blemishes, beginning with the ear: torn cartilage, a split, a hole the size of a legume, or desiccation. The Gemara derives, through the exegetical method of generalization-detail-generalization (כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל), exactly which kinds of blemishes the Torah means to include, then works out precise measurements for each one.

slides.title: 💰 New Mishna: Refunding Meat That Was Never Fit
slides.subtitle: A firstborn slaughtered without being shown to a Sage — what happens to the sale?
rows: Firstborn never shown to a Sage before slaughter
Buyers keep what they ate; seller refunds its price
Meat is buried; seller refunds its price
Cow later found to be a tereifa
Buyers keep what they ate; seller refunds its price
Buyers return the meat; seller may resell it to a gentile and refunds the balance
Buyers already sold/discarded the tereifa meat
Buyers pay the seller only the (lower) value of tereifa meat

callout.label: Extended baraita:
callout.text: The same rule applies to meat that turns out to be from an unexamined firstborn, produce that turns out untithed, or wine that turns out to be idolatrous libation wine.

slides.title: 🤢 How Much of a Refund? Repulsive vs. Non-Repulsive
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar qualifies the baraita

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: for repulsive items (נְבֵילוֹת, טְרֵיפוֹת, שְׁקָצִים) — full refund, since one is assumed not to have benefited. For non-repulsive items (בְּכוֹרוֹת, טְבָלִים, יֵין נֶסֶךְ) — only a deduction for benefit received.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But why deduct anything for firstborn meat? The buyer can say: 'What loss did I cause you? Without me, you had no right to eat it at all — it was unexamined and forbidden!'

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: This applies specifically where the cut sold came from a spot with the blemish itself: the seller can retort, 'Had you not eaten it, I would have shown the animal to a Sage and had it permitted' — following Rabbi Yehuda, who allows examination even after slaughter.

callout.label: Parallel logic:
callout.text: Untithed produce: 'I would have tithed it and eaten it myself.' Idolatrous wine mixed in: sellable to a gentile per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, so the seller lost real value.

slides.title: 📜 Deriving the Blemishes: 'Lame, Blind... Any Ill Blemish'
slides.subtitle: The exegetical method of generalization, detail, and generalization again

nodes.content: ❓ Deuteronomy 15:21 lists only 'lameness' and 'blindness' — how does the mishna permit slaughter for ear damage, splits, and holes too?
📖 The verse actually reads: 'if there be ANY blemish... lameness or blindness... ANY ill blemish' — a generalization, then a detail, then a generalization again
🔑 Rule: כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל includes anything similar to the detail — like lameness/blindness, blemishes must be visible and non-regenerating

columns.label: Included
columns.content: Visible, permanent blemishes — even ones that don't stop the animal from working, since 'any ill blemish' amplifies further

columns.label: Excluded
columns.content: Hidden blemishes (need visibility) and temporary blemishes (logic: if even redemption isn't allowed for a temporary blemish, certainly slaughter isn't)

callout.label: Key proof text:
callout.text: A baraita on Leviticus 27:11 shows that 'of which they may not bring an offering' teaches that only animals never fit for the altar (not temporarily unfit) may be redeemed — the same logic bars slaughtering a firstborn for a merely temporary blemish.

slides.title: 👂 The Ear's Disqualifying Blemishes
slides.subtitle: Four kinds of ear damage that permit slaughtering the firstborn
rows: Counts as a blemish; torn skin alone does not
Any size at all, whether by human hand or by natural cause
Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda: size of a lentil, slightly smaller
Pierced and produces no drop of blood
Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam: dry enough to crumble at a touch

callout.label: Fingernail measure:
callout.text: A qualifying tear or gap must be large enough 'that a fingernail will be retained on it' when passed over the spot.

slides.title: 📏 Pinning Down the Size of a Karshina
slides.subtitle: The Gemara cross-checks its measurements against unrelated impurity laws

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Hoshaya asks Rav Huna the Great: does 'the size of a karshina' mean a vetch that fits snugly, or one that can pass in and out of the hole?
2️⃣ Answer, by analogy from a similar measure: it means a hole large enough for the item to enter and exit freely

3️⃣ Elsewhere, Rav Ḥisda asks about the size of a skull-fragment deficiency (from the laws of corpse impurity) — told it is 'like a sela coin' — and objects that this collapses Beit Shammai's and Beit Hillel's measures into one
4️⃣ The comparison method itself is the point: precise halakhic measurements are pinned down by cross-referencing known measures from elsewhere in the Torah's system

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: Even a small technical term like 'karshina' gets careful, cross-referenced definition, since the exact size determines whether a firstborn may be slaughtered.

summary.principle: The mishna closes the laws of disqualified offerings with rules for refunding forbidden meat, then opens a new chapter deriving — through careful biblical exegesis and precise measurement — exactly which blemishes of the ear are severe, visible, and permanent enough to permit a firstborn's slaughter.

flowSteps.content: 💰 Firstborn/tereifa sold and later found forbidden: eaten meat stays eaten, seller refunds the price
🤢 Repulsive items get a full refund; non-repulsive items (like firstborn meat) only a partial deduction
📜 'Any blemish... lameness or blindness... any ill blemish' derives visible, permanent blemishes generally, via generalization-detail-generalization

columns.content: 👂 Torn cartilage, splits, and pierced holes of set sizes disqualify the ear
📏 Exact measures (karshina, lentil) are cross-checked against other impurity laws

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: only visible, permanent blemishes of a defined minimum size permit a firstborn's slaughter outside the Temple

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what happens to firstborn meat sold by someone who never showed the animal to a Sage before slaughtering it, if it has not yet been eaten?
o: The buyer keeps it and pays nothing further
It must be buried, and the seller must refund the money paid
It is given to the poor
It is sold to a gentile at full price
quiz.e: For meat not yet eaten, the mishna requires it to be buried (since it was never permitted) and the seller to return the purchase price.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, why does the seller of firstborn meat only deduct for benefit received rather than issue a full refund, unlike a seller of a carcass (neveila)?
o: Firstborn meat is considered a repulsive item like a carcass
Firstborn meat is a non-repulsive item, so the buyer is assumed to have genuinely benefited from eating it, unlike naturally repulsive items
There is no difference between the two cases
Firstborn meat can never be sold at all
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes repulsive items (full refund, since no benefit is assumed) from non-repulsive items like firstborn meat, produce, and idolatrous wine, where a deduction for actual benefit applies.

quiz.q: What exegetical method does the Gemara use to derive which blemishes, beyond lameness and blindness, disqualify a firstborn?
o: Gezeira shava (verbal analogy) alone
Generalization, detail, generalization (כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל) from 'any blemish... lameness or blindness... any ill blemish'
A fortiori (kal vachomer) reasoning only
Numerical calculation of the verse's letters
quiz.e: The verse's structure — a general term, a specific detail, then a general term again — teaches that any blemish similar to the detail (visible and permanent) is included.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara exclude a temporary blemish from permitting a firstborn's slaughter?
o: Temporary blemishes are not mentioned in the Torah at all
By logical inference: if even a temporary blemish does not allow redemption of a sacrificial animal, it certainly should not allow slaughtering a firstborn outside the Temple
Because only permanent injuries to the leg count
Because temporary blemishes are always hidden
quiz.e: The Gemara reasons that since redemption (a lesser departure from sanctity) is barred for a temporary blemish, slaughtering the animal outside the Temple certainly should be too.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what size hole in the firstborn's ear counts as a disqualifying blemish, and what is the disputing view?
o: Any size hole at all, with no dispute
The size of a karshina (bitter vetch); Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda says the size of a lentil
Only a hole the size of a human fist
The size of a sela coin, with no dispute
quiz.e: The first tanna requires a hole the size of a karshina (bitter vetch); Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, holds a slightly smaller lentil-sized hole suffices.
